tip: 'Farcela' means to manage or pull it off, a fixed idiom from 'fare' plus 'ce' plus 'la': 'possano farcela'.
'Andare' has an irregular conditional stem 'andr-': 'andresti' = you would go, not 'anderesti'.
'Secondo me' means 'in my opinion', literally 'according to me', the everyday way to open an opinion.
An object pronoun attaches to the end of an infinitive: 'dire' plus 'lo' becomes 'dirlo' (say it), and 'dire' drops its final -e.
The preposition 'a' merges with the article 'la' into 'alla': 'alla festa' = to the party.
'Problema' is masculine despite the -a ending, a Greek-origin word: 'il problema', 'i problemi'. Same for 'tema' and 'sistema'.
'È possibile che' plus the subjunctive: 'piova' from 'piovere'.
'Dovunque' (wherever) takes the subjunctive, not the indicative: 'dovunque tu sia', not 'sei'.
'Ovunque' (wherever) takes the subjunctive, so 'andare' becomes 'vada', not 'vai': 'ovunque tu vada'.
'Comunque' plus the subjunctive means 'however it turns out': 'comunque vada', whatever the outcome.
'Stare' is for a state you are in, 'essere' for what you are: 'sto attento' = I am being careful; 'sono malato' would mean I am ill.
'Che' plus the subjunctive on its own voices a wish: 'che tu sia benedetto' = may you be blessed.
For an action happening right now, use 'stare' plus the gerund: 'sta lavorando' (is working), not just 'lavora'.
Italian makes yes/no questions by intonation alone: 'sei fidanzata?' keeps the same word order as the statement.
The accented 'è', as in 'lui è dentro', means is; the plain 'e' with no accent means and.
Adjectives ending in -e like 'veloce' keep one form for both genders; a woman is also 'veloce'.
Adjectives ending in -e switch to -i in the plural: 'disponibile' becomes 'disponibili' for a group.
Adjectives match the speaker's gender: a man says 'curioso', a woman says 'curiosa'.
The subject pronoun is dropped here; the -i ending of 'sei' already tells you it means you.
In the past tense, 'già' (already) sits between 'hai' and the participle: 'hai già mangiato'.
'Ci' here means each other: 'ci sentiamo' is we hear from one another, a common way to say talk soon.
Use 'uno' instead of 'un' before s plus a consonant: 'uno sconto', 'uno studente'.
Masculine words starting with a vowel take 'lo', shortened before the vowel: 'l'ospedale', not 'lo ospedale'.
Italian often uses the present for near-future plans: 'fai domani' literally is do tomorrow.
Impersonal 'si' means one or you-in-general: 'si pronuncia' asks how it is pronounced.
'Lo' and 'la' drop their vowel before a noun starting with a vowel: 'l'ambulanza', not 'la ambulanza'.
'Le' is the polite to you here: 'quanto le devo' asks how much I owe you formally.
After 'vuoi', the second verb stays in the infinitive: 'vuoi uscire', not 'vuoi esci'.
A past participle used as an adjective agrees in gender: 'colazione' is feminine, so 'compresa' ends in -a.
Some set phrases drop the article: 'a scuola' means at school, with no 'la' needed.
